glossary.definition: The collection of reachable points, interfaces, accounts, services, devices, applications, and human processes that an attacker might target.
The route or method an attacker uses to reach a target, such as a phishing message, exposed service, or removable device.
Unauthorized transfer of data out of a system or organization.
The code, command, or content that performs the malicious action after delivery or exploitation.
Movement from one compromised system or account to additional systems or resources inside an environment.
A user or server device connected to a network, such as a laptop, workstation, or server.
Low-level software embedded in hardware that controls how the device operates.
Still present but no longer recommended because a safer or newer option should be used.
An approved reference configuration used to define the expected secure state of a system.

authoring_notes: Authored for the api-call branch content schema. Uses CompTIA's official objective IDs 2.1-2.5 as skill IDs. Definition-first nodes, small progressive tables, scenario-first attack analysis, and classification-heavy taxonomy practice are intentional. Indicators are taught as evidence to correlate rather than proof. Mitigation questions focus on matching controls to a stated risk instead of treating any control as universally sufficient.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What are you trying to identify?

reveal.text: A threat actor is a person or group that can cause harm. Attributes describe the actor's capability and position; motivation explains why the actor acts.

columns.title: Actor
items: Who is acting?
Example: organized crime

columns.title: Attributes
items: What capability or access do they have?
Example: internal, well-funded

columns.title: Motivation
items: Why are they acting?
Example: financial gain

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST CSRC Glossary — Threat Actor

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Nation-state and organized crime?

reveal.text: Nation-state actors are linked to a government and may pursue strategic goals such as espionage or disruption. Organized crime is coordinated criminal activity that commonly pursues profit or leverage.

cells.pattern: May have substantial resources, intelligence access, and long-term objectives
Coordinated criminal activity, often with specialized roles

prompts.label: DO NOT OVERFIT
prompts.placeholder: Does actor type guarantee motive?

reveal.text: No. Actor types have common patterns, but you should use scenario evidence such as targets, resources, behavior, and stated goals instead of assuming a motive from the label alone.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Hacktivist and unskilled attacker?

reveal.text: A hacktivist acts to advance a cause or belief. An unskilled attacker has limited expertise and often relies on tools or instructions created by others.

columns.title: Hacktivist
items: Usually driven by a cause or belief
Skill and resources can vary

columns.title: Unskilled attacker
items: Limited expertise
Often relies on tools or instructions created by others

prompts.label: SCENARIO CLUE
prompts.placeholder: What wording should catch your attention?

reveal.text: A public cause, protest, or ideological message points toward hacktivist motivation. Copying a public exploit with little understanding points toward an unskilled attacker.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Insider threat and shadow IT?

reveal.text: An insider threat comes from someone with legitimate internal access or trust, including malicious, careless, or compromised insiders. Shadow IT is technology used without required organizational approval or visibility.

spans.text: without required organizational approval or visibility

cells.meaning: Risk created by someone with legitimate internal access or trust
cells.clue: Employee, contractor, or partner misuses or exposes access

cells.meaning: Technology used without required organizational approval or visibility
cells.clue: Teams adopt unapproved SaaS, devices, or tools

prompts.label: IMPORTANT
prompts.placeholder: Does internal mean malicious?

reveal.text: No. Insider risk can be malicious, negligent, accidental, or caused by a compromised account. Shadow IT can also be well-intentioned while still creating unmanaged risk.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: Hardware, software, or cloud services used without the required approval, inventory, or security oversight of the organization.

nodes.title: Actor attributes: internal, funding, and capability

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Actor attributes: internal, funding, and capability?

reveal.text: Threat-actor attributes describe the actor's position, resources, and technical capability. They help you profile an actor without assuming identity or motivation from one clue.

prompts.label: PROFILE THE ACTOR
prompts.placeholder: What attributes matter?

items: Internal vs. external: does the actor already have trusted access or operate from outside?
Resources/funding: how much money, infrastructure, time, and personnel can support the activity?
Sophistication/capability: how advanced are the actor's tools, tradecraft, and ability to evade defenses?

reveal.text: Do not identify an actor from one clue. Combine access position, resources, capability, target selection, and motivation.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Threat actor motivations?

reveal.text: A threat actor's motivation is the reason the actor takes action. Common motives include money, espionage, revenge, ideology, disruption, data theft, blackmail, ethics, and war.

prompts.label: NUANCE
prompts.placeholder: What does ethical mean here?

reveal.text: The objectives include ethical motivation. In a scenario, it can describe authorized or responsible security research. Authorization still matters: good intent does not automatically make an action permitted.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

modules.title: Recognize threat vectors and attack surfaces

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Threat vector vs. attack surface?

reveal.text: A threat vector is the path or method an attacker uses to reach a target. An attack surface is the full set of reachable people, accounts, services, devices, and interfaces that could be attacked.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: How are these different?

columns.title: Threat vector
items: The path or method used to reach a target
Examples: phishing email, exposed service, USB device

columns.title: Attack surface
items: All reachable points that could be attacked
Examples: accounts, ports, apps, devices, people

reveal.text: Vector is the route in. Attack surface is the collection of places an attacker might try.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: Message, image, file, voice, and removable-device vectors

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Message, image, file, voice, and removable-device vectors?

reveal.text: A delivery channel is the medium used to carry a lure, request, or malicious content to a target. Security+ includes message, image, file, voice, and removable-device vectors.

cells.clue: Email, SMS, or instant message delivers a lure, link, or request
An image is used to carry or present malicious/deceptive content
A document, archive, executable, or other file delivers the attack
The attacker persuades the target in a phone or voice conversation
USB or other removable media carries data or malicious content

reveal.text: Classify by the delivery path first. The same social-engineering goal can arrive through different channels.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Phishing, smishing, and vishing?

reveal.text: Phishing uses deceptive messages or sites to manipulate people. Smishing is phishing through SMS/text messages, while vishing uses voice calls.
The defining difference among smishing and vishing is the communication channel, not whether the message is targeted or sophisticated.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
CISA — Phishing Guidance

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Misinformation, disinformation, and pretexting?

reveal.text: Misinformation is false information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately deceptive information, while pretexting uses a fabricated story or role to manipulate someone.

cells.meaning: False or inaccurate information shared without an intent to deceive
False or manipulated information deliberately used to deceive
A fabricated story or role used to persuade someone to reveal information or take an action

reveal.text: For misinformation vs. disinformation, ask about intent. For pretexting, look for a made-up identity, situation, or business reason.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Impersonation, BEC, and brand impersonation?

reveal.text: Impersonation pretends to be a trusted person or organization. Business email compromise (BEC) abuses business identity or email to induce fraud, while brand impersonation copies a trusted brand.

cells.focus: Pretend to be a trusted person or organization
Use or imitate business email identity to induce fraudulent actions, often payments or data release
Copy a trusted brand's name, look, or identity to deceive users

reveal.text: A message that appears to come from an executive or supplier and urgently changes payment instructions is a classic BEC pattern.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Watering-hole and typosquatting attacks?

reveal.text: A watering-hole attack compromises a site that intended targets already visit. Typosquatting uses a misspelled or look-alike domain to send victims to the wrong site.

columns.title: Watering hole
items: Compromise a site the intended targets already visit
Target comes to the compromised site

columns.title: Typosquatting
items: Use a misspelled or look-alike domain
Victim reaches the wrong site through a typo or deceptive link

reveal.text: If attackers compromise a niche site used by a target group, think watering hole. If the domain itself is deceptively similar, think typosquatting.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Vulnerable and unsupported software?

reveal.text: Vulnerable software contains a weakness that can be exploited or triggered. Unsupported software is especially risky because the vendor may no longer provide security fixes.

items: Vulnerable software exposes a weakness that an attacker can reach or trigger.
Unsupported systems and applications may no longer receive vendor security fixes.
Client-based and agentless access models create different software footprints; inventory what is installed, reachable, and maintained.

reveal.text: Internet-facing services, old versions, unsupported products, and forgotten software expand the attack surface.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
CISA/NSA — Top Ten Cybersecurity Misconfigurations

nodes.title: Networks, open ports, default credentials, and supply chain

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Networks, open ports, default credentials, and supply chain?

reveal.text: Attack surfaces grow when networks, services, credentials, or trusted suppliers expose a path into the environment. Defenders should identify what is reachable, trusted, and maintained.

cells.surface: Unsecure wireless, wired, or Bluetooth network
cells.risk: Traffic or access may be exposed to unauthorized parties
Reachable services can be probed or exploited
Known or guessable credentials may grant immediate access
A trusted dependency can become an indirect path into the organization

reveal.text: Ask what is reachable, trusted, and maintained. An attack path can be direct through your systems or indirect through a trusted supplier.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What is a vulnerability?

reveal.text: A vulnerability is a weakness in technology, configuration, process, or implementation that a threat can exploit or trigger to cause harm.

columns.title: Threat
items: Potential cause of harm

columns.title: Vulnerability
items: Weakness that can be exploited or triggered

columns.title: Attack
items: Action that attempts to exploit, disrupt, or compromise

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST CSRC Glossary — Vulnerability

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Memory injection and buffer overflow?

reveal.text: Memory injection places malicious code or content into a running process's memory. A buffer overflow writes more data than a buffer can hold and can overwrite nearby memory.

columns.title: Memory injection
items: Malicious code or content is placed into the memory of a running process
Goal may be to execute inside that process

columns.title: Buffer overflow
items: More data is written than a buffer can hold
Adjacent memory can be overwritten or corrupted

reveal.text: A buffer overflow is a specific bounds-handling failure. Memory injection is broader and focuses on placing malicious content into process memory.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: TIMING BUG
prompts.placeholder: What is the core problem?

reveal.text: A race condition happens when security or correctness depends on timing. In a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOC/TOU) flaw, the checked state changes before the program uses it.

items: Program checks a resource or condition
Another actor changes the resource
Program assumes the old checked state is still true
Program uses the changed resource and gets an unsafe result

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
MITRE CWE-367 — Time-of-check Time-of-use Race Condition

glossary.definition: A flaw in which the outcome depends on timing or ordering between operations that can occur concurrently.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Malicious updates and OS-based vulnerabilities?

reveal.text: A malicious update is an intentionally compromised software update or update path. An operating-system vulnerability is a weakness in the OS or its configuration that can affect software running on it.

spans.text: compromised software update or update path

columns.title: Malicious update
items: An update package or delivery path is intentionally compromised
Trust in the update process is abused

columns.title: OS-based vulnerability
items: A weakness in the operating system or its configuration
Can affect many applications that rely on the OS

reveal.text: Unexpected signed-update behavior, compromised distribution infrastructure, unpatched OS flaws, or insecure OS configuration can all be relevant clues.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about SQL injection and cross-site scripting?

reveal.text: SQL injection (SQLi) lets untrusted input alter a database query. Cross-site scripting (XSS) causes untrusted content to execute as script in a user's browser context.

cells.core idea: Untrusted input changes the meaning of a database query
Untrusted content is rendered so it executes as script in a user's browser

reveal.text: SQLi changes a query sent to the database. XSS causes untrusted content to execute in a browser context.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
OWASP — SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
OWASP — Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Firmware, end-of-life, and legacy hardware?

reveal.text: Firmware is low-level software embedded in hardware. End-of-life means vendor support has ended, while legacy hardware is older technology still kept for compatibility or business reasons.

cells.meaning: Low-level software embedded in hardware; flaws or outdated firmware can expose the device
Vendor support has ended, so security fixes may no longer be provided
Older technology retained for compatibility or business reasons; it may or may not already be end-of-life

reveal.text: End-of-life is about vendor support status. Legacy means old or inherited technology; do not assume those terms are always identical.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
CISA/NSA — Top Ten Cybersecurity Misconfigurations

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Virtualization vulnerabilities?

reveal.text: Virtualization vulnerabilities break or misuse isolation between virtual resources. VM escape crosses the guest boundary, while unsafe resource reuse can expose data left by a previous tenant or workload.

columns.title: VM escape
items: A guest breaks isolation and affects the hypervisor, host, or another guest

columns.title: Resource reuse
items: Reused storage or memory can expose residual data if it is not properly cleared or isolated

reveal.text: Virtualization security depends on isolation. VM escape breaks the boundary; unsafe resource reuse leaks across the boundary.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: Cloud, supply-chain, cryptographic, and misconfiguration vulnerabilities

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Cloud, supply-chain, cryptographic, and misconfiguration vulnerabilities?

reveal.text: Cloud-specific, supply-chain, cryptographic, and configuration weaknesses are different vulnerability classes. Identify where the weakness originates before choosing a mitigation.

cells.examples: Overly broad permissions, exposed storage, insecure service configuration
Compromised service, hardware, or software provider
Weak algorithms, poor key handling, weak randomness, insecure implementation
Unsafe defaults, excessive exposure, incorrect permissions

reveal.text: When the product itself is sound but settings expose data or access, think misconfiguration. When a trusted provider introduces the weakness, think supply chain.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Sideloading, jailbreaking, and zero-day vulnerabilities?

reveal.text: Sideloading installs an app outside the approved distribution path. Jailbreaking or rooting bypasses platform restrictions, while a zero-day is exploited before defenders have a normal patching advantage.

cells.meaning: Installing an application from outside the normal approved app-distribution path
Removing or bypassing platform restrictions to gain deeper control; this can weaken built-in protections
A previously unknown vulnerability being exploited before defenders have a normal patching advantage

reveal.text: A zero-day describes the defender's lack of prior knowledge or patch opportunity, not a guarantee that the exploit is sophisticated or unstoppable.

spans.text: lack of prior knowledge or patch opportunity

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST CSRC Glossary — Zero-day Attack

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Attack type vs. indicator?

reveal.text: An attack type describes what an adversary is doing. An indicator is evidence that may point to malicious activity, but one indicator alone is rarely proof.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What are you analyzing?

columns.title: Attack/activity
items: What the adversary is doing
Example: password spraying

columns.title: Indicator
items: Evidence that may point to malicious activity
Example: many failed logins across accounts

reveal.text: One indicator rarely proves an attack by itself. Correlate identity, network, endpoint, application, and timing evidence.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Ransomware, trojan, worm, virus?

reveal.text: Malware is software or code used to cause harm or unauthorized activity. Ransomware, trojans, worms, and viruses differ mainly in what they do and how they spread.

spans.text: what they do and how they spread

cells.remember: Denies access or encrypts data to extort the victim; may also steal data
Pretends to be legitimate or desirable software
Attaches to a host file/program and spreads when the host executes

reveal.text: If self-propagation without a user launching an infected host is the key clue, think worm rather than virus.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
CISA — #StopRansomware Guide

nodes.title: Spyware, keylogger, logic bomb, rootkit, and bloatware

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Spyware, keylogger, logic bomb, rootkit, and bloatware?

reveal.text: Malware and unwanted software can spy, capture input, trigger on a condition, hide privileged activity, or consume resources. The behavior is the strongest clue to the correct term.

cells.behavior: Triggers an action when a specified condition is met
Maintains privileged, stealthy control and can hide malicious activity
Unwanted or excessive software that consumes resources; not every instance is malicious

reveal.text: Bloatware can create risk or reduce performance, but the term does not automatically mean intentionally malicious code.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: Physical brute force, RFID cloning, and environmental attacks

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Physical brute force, RFID cloning, and environmental attacks?

reveal.text: Physical attacks target facilities, devices, or physical credentials rather than only software. Security+ includes physical brute force, RFID cloning, and environmental attacks.

cells.clue: Force is used against a lock, door, enclosure, or other physical barrier
An RFID credential or identifier is copied and reused
Power, temperature, water, fire, or other environmental conditions are used or manipulated to disrupt systems

reveal.text: CompTIA also lists brute force under password attacks. Use the context: forcing a barrier is physical; guessing credentials is a password attack.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: DDoS, DNS, wireless, on-path, and credential replay

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about DDoS, DNS, wireless, on-path, and credential replay?

reveal.text: Network attacks target communication, name resolution, availability, wireless access, or authentication traffic. Identify what part of the communication path is being abused.

cells.core idea: Many hosts overwhelm or exhaust a target's resources
Abuse or manipulate name-resolution infrastructure or responses
Exploit radio-based network access or trust
Attacker positions between communicating parties to observe or alter traffic
Captured authentication material or messages are reused to impersonate a legitimate party

reveal.text: DDoS attacks availability. On-path attacks communication trust. Replay attacks reuse something valid that was captured earlier.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST CSRC Glossary — Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS)
NIST CSRC Glossary — Man-in-the-Middle Attack
NIST CSRC Glossary — Replay Attack

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Reflected and amplified DDoS?

reveal.text: Reflection sends third-party replies toward a spoofed victim. Amplification makes the reply much larger than the request; an attack can use both techniques together.

columns.title: Reflected
items: Attacker spoofs the victim as the source
Third-party systems send replies toward the victim

columns.title: Amplified
items: A small request causes a much larger response
Traffic volume grows before it hits the victim

reveal.text: A DDoS can be both reflected and amplified: spoofed requests cause many third parties to send larger replies to the victim.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: Injection, overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery, and directory traversal

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Injection, overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery, and directory traversal?

reveal.text: Application attacks exploit how software handles input, memory, authorization, requests, identities, or file paths. The violated boundary usually reveals the attack type.

cells.clue: Untrusted data changes commands or interpreter behavior
Excess data overwrites memory beyond a buffer
A previously valid request/message is captured and resent
An actor gains permissions beyond the starting authorization
Data, identity, request, or object is falsified to appear legitimate
Path manipulation reaches files outside the intended directory

reveal.text: Ask what boundary is being crossed: interpreter boundary, memory boundary, authorization boundary, or filesystem path boundary.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Downgrade, collision, and birthday attacks?

reveal.text: Cryptographic attacks try to weaken negotiation or exploit properties of cryptographic functions. Security+ includes downgrade, collision, and birthday attacks.

cells.core idea: Force or negotiate a weaker protocol, algorithm, or security mode
Find two different inputs that produce the same hash output
Exploit collision probability; collisions become likely after far fewer than all possible outputs are tried

reveal.text: If the scenario focuses on two different messages sharing a digest, think collision. Birthday attacks are a probabilistic way to search for collisions.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST CSRC Glossary — Collision

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Password spraying vs. brute force?

reveal.text: Password spraying tries a small number of passwords across many accounts. Brute force tries many guesses against a password, key, or account until one works.

columns.title: Password spraying
items: Try a small set of common passwords across many accounts
Designed to avoid repeated failures on one account

columns.title: Brute force
items: Try many candidate passwords or keys until one works
Often produces concentrated repeated guessing

reveal.text: Many accounts each receiving a few similar guesses suggests spraying. Many guesses against one account suggests brute force.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
CISA — #StopRansomware Guide

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Indicators of malicious activity?

reveal.text: Indicators are observable signs that may suggest malicious activity, such as unusual sessions, missing logs, blocked content, lockouts, or abnormal resource use. Correlation makes an indicator more meaningful.

spans.text: Correlation makes an indicator more meaningful

cells.what it can suggest: Repeated failed authentication or policy-triggered blocking
The same identity may be active from unexpected places or devices
A security control stopped suspicious content or access
Logins occur too far apart geographically to be physically plausible in the time available
CPU, memory, storage, or bandwidth spikes may accompany malicious activity
DoS, ransomware, failure, or unauthorized changes may be affecting service
Activity occurs at an unusual time or outside expected operational patterns
Observed data matches a known indicator described in trusted advisories or threat intelligence
Logging failure, misconfiguration, or possible tampering; investigate context

reveal.text: Correlate multiple indicators with normal baselines. An impossible-travel alert plus a new device and concurrent session is stronger evidence than any one signal alone.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: Choose mitigation by the risk you need to reduce

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What is mitigation?

reveal.text: A mitigation is a safeguard or action that reduces the likelihood or impact of a threat or vulnerability. Choose it based on the attack path and asset at risk.

spans.text: attack path and asset at risk

items: Identify the threat or weakness
Identify what an attacker can reach or do
Choose a control that directly reduces that path or impact
Verify that the control is applied and monitored

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Segmentation and isolation?

reveal.text: Segmentation divides systems into controlled communication zones. Isolation separates a system more completely, which is useful for quarantine or especially high-risk assets.

columns.title: Segmentation
items: Divide networks or systems into controlled zones
Restrict which zones can communicate
Reduces lateral movement and blast radius

columns.title: Isolation
items: Separate a system or workload more completely
Useful for quarantine or high-risk assets
Stronger separation than ordinary segmentation

reveal.text: Segmentation limits paths. Isolation removes or sharply narrows paths.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST — Security Measures for EO-Critical Software Use

nodes.title: ACLs, permissions, allow lists, and least privilege

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about ACLs, permissions, allow lists, and least privilege?

reveal.text: Access controls limit what identities, traffic, or software are allowed to do. ACLs, permissions, application allow lists, and least privilege solve different parts of that problem.

prompts.label: CONTROL WHO OR WHAT CAN ACT

cells.job: Permit or deny access based on defined rules for a resource, interface, or traffic flow
Define what an identity can read, write, execute, or manage
Allow only approved applications to run
Give users and processes only the access needed for their assigned tasks

reveal.text: ACLs and permissions enforce access decisions. Allow lists reduce what software can execute. Least privilege reduces the damage a compromised identity can cause.

spans.text: damage a compromised identity can cause

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 — Least Privilege and Least Functionality

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Patching, configuration enforcement, and decommissioning?

reveal.text: Patching fixes known software flaws. Configuration enforcement keeps systems aligned with an approved secure state, while decommissioning safely removes systems that should no longer exist.

cells.purpose: Correct known flaws or update vulnerable components
Keep systems aligned with an approved secure baseline
Remove systems that are no longer needed or supportable, including access and residual data

reveal.text: Patch what should remain. Enforce the secure state. Retire what should no longer exist.

spans.text: Retire what should no longer exist

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
CISA/NSA — Top Ten Cybersecurity Misconfigurations
NIST NCCoE — Hardening Information

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Encryption and monitoring as mitigations?

reveal.text: Encryption protects data confidentiality when implemented correctly. Monitoring collects and analyzes activity so suspicious behavior can be detected and investigated.

columns.title: Encryption
items: Protects confidentiality of data when implemented correctly
Does not by itself stop malware, bad authorization, or service disruption

columns.title: Monitoring
items: Collects and analyzes activity so suspicious behavior can be detected and investigated
Detection is useful only when signals are reviewed and acted on

reveal.text: No single mitigation solves every attack. Encryption protects data confidentiality; monitoring helps detect activity. Layer controls around the actual risk.

spans.text: No single mitigation solves every attack

prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Host hardening techniques?

reveal.text: Host hardening reduces a system's attack surface and strengthens the configuration that remains. Typical steps include endpoint protection, host firewalls, HIPS, secure passwords, and removing unnecessary services or software.

items: Enable appropriate encryption.
Install endpoint protection and a host-based firewall.
Use HIPS where host-based prevention is needed.
Disable unnecessary ports and protocols.
Change default passwords.
Remove unnecessary software.

reveal.text: Hardening means removing unnecessary exposure and strengthening the configuration of what must remain.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about Layer mitigations around likely attack paths?

reveal.text: Layered mitigation combines controls so one failure does not expose the whole system. Start with the stated weakness, then add only controls that directly reduce the attack path or impact.

spans.text: one failure does not expose the whole system

items: Patch or upgrade if support exists
Restrict access with segmentation and ACLs
Use least privilege and remove default credentials
Disable unnecessary services and software
Monitor the host and network for suspicious activity
Decommission the system when it is no longer required

reveal.text: When a scenario asks for the BEST mitigation, choose the control that most directly addresses the stated weakness. Add layers only when the question asks for multiple controls.
